summary: Sieve is a language for filtering email on the server. This extension adds an include command so one Sieve script can pull in another, which makes large scripts easier to manage. Users can include their own scripts or site-wide ones and build libraries of reusable rules.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of writing the same mail sorting rules again and again, you keep them in separate cards and tell your script to also read this card.

questions: how to include one sieve script in another
what is the sieve include extension
subtitle: Lets one Sieve email filter script pull in another, with shared variables and personal or site-wide libraries.

tldr.problem: Large Sieve filter scripts are hard to manage, and people want to reuse pieces such as a vacation notice or a site-wide spam check without copying them.
tldr.mechanism: The include extension adds an include command that runs another script at that point, from the user's personal repository or a site-wide global one, plus return and global commands for control flow and shared variables.
tldr.outcome: Users and sites can build libraries of scripts, with rules about nesting, recursion, missing scripts and variable scope that keep included scripts from interfering with each other.

today: RFC 6609 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. IANA added the include capability to its Sieve Extensions registry.

sections.title: Why Include Scripts
sections.content:
It is convenient to break Sieve (RFC 5228) scripts into smaller reusable parts. The RFC's example is a user with a default script and a special vacation script. Rather than editing the default script to add or remove a vacation command, the user can have a vacation script that runs vacation and then includes the default script.

This document defines the include extension, which lets one script include another. The capability name include must be listed in require if a script uses include, return or global.
sections.plainLanguage: If you have a rule list you want to reuse, you point to it instead of copying it out again.

sections.title: General Rules for Included Scripts
sections.content:
The RFC defines the immediate script (the one being executed) and the including script (the one whose include statement brought it in). A script execution runs from the active script through all included scripts to the final disposition of the message.

Implementations MAY limit nesting but MUST allow at least three levels, including the top-level script. Exceeding the limit is an error, raised at upload or execution, and an implicit keep MUST then run so no message is lost. Recursive inclusion, direct or indirect, MUST NOT be allowed, and is an error at execution time, not at upload time. A missing script is likewise an error at execution time unless :optional is used. Checking only at execution avoids forcing authors to upload scripts in a particular order.

Each script needs its own require statements. A require neither inherits nor passes on capabilities to other scripts.
sections.plainLanguage: You can put cards inside cards, but not too deep, and a card must never lead back to itself. If a card is missing, the reader stops with an error and keeps your mail safe.

sections.title: The include and return Commands
sections.content:
Usage: include [LOCATION] [":once"] [":optional"] <value: string>. The script name must be a constant string, so variables are not expanded in it, and names follow the restrictions of ManageSieve (RFC 5804).

  • :personal (the default) means the script is in the user's own repository.
  • :global means it is in a site-wide repository available to all users.
  • :once includes the script only if it has not already been included during this execution. It is RECOMMENDED for scripts doing general duties such as declaring globals or checking the environment.
  • :optional makes a missing script a no-op instead of an error.

include may appear anywhere a control structure is legal, including inside an if block. A stop in an included script halts all processing, including the scripts that include it. The return command stops only the immediate script and gives control back to the including script. In the main script, return acts like stop.
sections.plainLanguage: An include is like saying read that other card now. Return means finish this card and go back to the one that sent you. Stop means stop reading everything.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content: The RFC's example has a user whose default script includes four others: a personal always_allow script that keeps mail from certain senders, a global spam_tests script maintained by the site administrator, a personal spam_tests script for user-specific rejects, and a mailing_lists script that files list mail into mailboxes. Global and personal scripts may share a name because the location selects which one is meant.
sections.plainLanguage: One main card says: check the friends list, then the school's spam rules, then my own spam rules, then sort the mailing lists.

sections.title: Variables and the global Command
sections.content:
With the variables extension (RFC 5229), the same variable name in two scripts could clash. So variables are private to the immediate script by default. The global command, usable only when both include and variables are required, declares names shared among scripts. A non-global variable may have the same name as a global one with no interaction.

Names must be constant strings; match variables and namespace prefixes are not allowed, and declaring global a name already set locally is an error. A global variable with no value evaluates to an empty string. The RFC also defines a global variables namespace: set "global.name" ... and global "name" refer to the same variable. That namespace has no sub-namespaces, and using it without requiring include is an error.

The worked example passes data this way: the top-level script sets a test variable, includes subject_tests twice, and reads back test_mailbox to decide which mailbox to file into.
sections.plainLanguage: Each card has its own private notepad. If cards must share a note, they both write it on a shared whiteboard first.

sections.title: Interaction with Other Extensions
sections.content: With editheader (RFC 5293), header changes MUST pass both into and out of included scripts. With the MIME extension (RFC 5703), an included script sees the current MIME part as if it were the whole message, and a break in it cannot end the other script's foreverypart loop. It can use return and global variables to pass results back. With reject (RFC 5429), calling reject or ereject sets the reject action and execution continues, and the rejection applies to the whole message, not one MIME part.
sections.plainLanguage: Other add-ons keep working inside cards, and changes made in one card are seen by the next.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations MUST secure the global script repository against unauthorized changes. A site might let only administrators modify global scripts, and sites are advised against giving every user write access.

Script names MUST be checked for validity and permissions before inclusion, and for safety with the storage system, so a malicious user cannot reach files the mail server can access. The RFC calls include "./../..//etc/passwd" hostile. Beyond that, no new considerations arise beyond those in RFC 5228 and RFC 5229.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted people should edit the shared cards, and nobody should be able to trick the reader into opening files that are not cards.

items.title: :personal
items.text: Script comes from the user's own repository. This is the default.

items.title: :global
items.text: Script comes from the site-wide repository.

items.title: :once
items.text: Skip the include if the script was already included during this execution.

items.title: :optional
items.text: A missing script is ignored instead of causing an error.
